models.best: Inferred from its principle that care is repaid through reciprocal gifts, so the sick are supported by kin and neighbours who expect help back, and healers are rewarded in kind rather than by fees. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that favours create obligations, so care goes first to those who can return help, while strangers and people without kin or neighbours who can give support may be left without treatment. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mauss, The Gift (1925)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that each household balances its work against its needs, so families fund care from their own labour and stores, timing treatment around the farm year. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production serves consumption, so a household short of labour cannot spare a member to be cared for, and a sick person with no household to work the land may be left without funds. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chayanov, The Theory of Peasant Economy (1925)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a central authority collects surplus and redistributes it, so a central store can pay for healers and infirmaries that serve workers and officials from common funds. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that allocation follows rank, so the central store may pay for care mainly for officials and favoured households, while ordinary workers pay in tribute or taxes and receive little back. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that output is sold through trade, so an owner pays for treatment only where it keeps up output that can be sold, and costs are held to what the work returns. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the enslaved are denied education and property, so they have no means to pay for or choose their own care, and sickness or injury falls on them alone with no route to treatment. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (1944)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a lord gives protection and land in return for service, so the manor supplies some care for its tenants from its own resources, paid in kind. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that services are owed to a lord, so care is tied to bonded service: a tenant who falls ill still owes labour and rent, and the children of manorial tenants cannot leave the manor for training or treatment. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Bloch, Feudal Society (1939-1940)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that statutes fix training and quality, so guild members may pool dues under the statutes to support members who fall sick, and masters answer for the members they admit. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that masters control entry, so the sick and newcomers outside the guild have no claim on its funds, and a closed body decides who may practise and who may be treated. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Boileau, Le Livre des métiers (c. 1268)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state aims at a trade surplus, so it may fund the health of workers, soldiers and seamen whose service serves national trade goals. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state regulates production toward national gain, so care is paid mainly where it serves trade or the army, and spending on people outside those goals falls away; colonial labour may carry much of the cost. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mun, England's Treasure by Forraign Trade (1664)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a single tax on the rent of land should fund the state, so health spending comes from land rent and the tax falls on no labour, trade or capital. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that only agriculture makes a net product, so a land-rent tax is the sole source of revenue; when rents fall or the tax is poorly collected, care for town and non-farm workers is thin, with no other funding to fall back on. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Quesnay, Tableau économique (1758)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that competition among private providers and insurers lowers prices and raises quality, so patients pay directly or through private insurance, and the state only enforces contracts. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state stays out, so people who cannot buy insurance have no public cover, and providers may charge what the sick can pay, leaving the poor with the least care. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Smith, The Wealth of Nations (1776)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that prices carry knowledge spread across many people, so insurers and providers compete on visible prices that show what care costs, and no planner sets hospital budgets. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that credit expansion distorts production, so budgets paid for with cheap credit can build hospitals and capacity that cannot be paid for later, and the cost falls on patients and taxpayers. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Menger, Grundsätze der Volkswirthschaftslehre (1871)

models.best: The case Singapore's MediSave account from 1984 is a compulsory savings account for health care, with employers and employees each paying 3 per cent of wages at the start, so saving rather than general taxation meets the cost. The launch date and rates come from one secondary page and have not been confirmed against official records.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state's role shrinks and controls on markets are removed, so people who lose income or fall ill may have no public cover and must pay fees at the point of care, which can keep the sick from treatment. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (1962)

models.best: The case Oregon's Medicaid lottery, 2008 gave a limited number of people places to apply for Medicaid. Secondary summaries report that diagnoses of diabetes rose, that the share screening positive for depression fell by about nine percentage points, and that employment and earnings did not change significantly; blood pressure, cholesterol and HbA1c showed no significant change.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that spending falls in booms and rises in slumps, so public coverage may be widened in downturns and cut back in strong years, and treatment may swing with the business cycle. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Keynes, The General Theory (1936)

models.best: The case Germany's sickness insurance law of 1883 took effect on 1 December 1883, an early example of social insurance under a legal order. The case gives no coverage figure, because early coverage estimates differ between sources.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a legal order curbs monopoly, so if insurers or providers merge into dominant blocs, they may set fees and limit who is covered, leaving patients fewer options and higher bills. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Müller-Armack, Wirtschaftslenkung und Marktwirtschaft (1947)

models.best: In the case The National Health Service, 1948, care began on 5 July 1948 under the National Health Service Act of 1946, funded from general taxation and free at the point of use. The sources do not cover the health services of the devolved nations.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that universal services are financed by high taxes, so when budgets tighten, pressure may build to cut the service or add charges, and a universal promise can be narrowed over time. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Saltsjöbaden Agreement (1938)

models.best: The case Taiwan's national health insurance from 1995 launched a single-payer national scheme in March 1995. A 2010 study reports that the insured share rose from about 57 per cent to between 98 and 99 per cent, though sources give different baselines, so the 57 per cent figure is approximate.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state picks favoured fields, so a single state purchaser may favour chosen hospitals and drugs, and care in other fields is starved, leaving some providers and patients shut out. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Johnson, MITI and the Japanese Miracle (1982)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the rent of land should fund public services, so a tax on the value of land pays for health care and spares wages and firms from a separate levy. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a land tax is the main revenue, so if land values are misjudged or the tax is weakly enforced, health funds may fall short, and landowners may still pass some costs on to tenants. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: George, Progress and Poverty (1879)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that cooperative communities share work and goods, so members pool their means to care for the sick and aged within the association, and no fee is charged for it. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that planned associations are built by example, so care depends on each community's health and may be withdrawn when a community fails or its members leave, leaving the sick without support. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Owen, A New View of Society (1813)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that mutual credit and free contracts let workers keep the value of their work, so members pay into mutual funds they run together, with no rent or interest adding to the cost of care. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that membership is voluntary, so people who are not members of a mutual fund, or who fall ill before they can join, have no cover, and a small fund may not pool enough risk to pay for care. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Proudhon, What Is Property? (1840)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that members own and control the firms and share the surplus, so a health cooperative sets its fees by member vote and returns any surplus to the members who use its services. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that each member has one vote, so a cooperative's rules can exclude outsiders and those who cannot pay in, and a surplus shared among members may be paid out rather than held for care in lean years. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers (1844)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that goods are shared by need within federated communes, so care is given free to anyone who needs it, paid for from what the communes make together, with no wage or fee. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there is no state and no contract, so a commune that lacks the means to treat illness has no body to call on for funds, and the sick depend on the goodwill of their neighbours. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kropotkin, The Conquest of Bread (1892)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers' organisations run industry directly, so a fund run by the unions pays for care, and workers decide how health contributions are spent through their own bodies. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that strikes are the main weapon, so care funded by union dues may be drawn into industrial disputes, and members who strike may lose cover, leaving workers and families without treatment during a conflict. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Founding of the French CGT (1895)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a national minimum is provided through public enterprise, so every person is covered by public health services paid from the national budget and run by local and national bodies. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: In the case The National Health Service, 1948, care was funded from general taxation and was free at the point of use, but in 1951 charges for some dental and optical items were introduced in Hugh Gaitskell's budget, and Aneurin Bevan resigned from the government in protest. Inferred from its principle that the national minimum is paid from the national budget, it depends on each budget. The 1951 charges show how a free service can be cut back by a budget. The sources do not cover the devolved nations. Source: Warwick University Library, welfare state documents on the NHS (secondary)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers and consumers share control of industry through guild-like councils, so the councils help decide how health funds are spent, with the state as one partner among several. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that councils of workers and consumers share control, so a health service run by competing councils may split along trade lines, with some trades covered well and others left out, and the state's share of the duty unclear. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Cole, Self-Government in Industry (1917)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state owns industry and central plans set output and investment, so care is paid for from the state budget, and the plan decides how much of it is spent on health. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: In the case The Soviet health system under Semashko, from 1918, a July 1918 decree put health facilities under state ownership and declared care free to everyone, but a review describes the system as underfunded and heavily reliant on inpatient care. Another paper dates the start of implementation to the late 1920s, and sources disagree on the scope of Semashko's post and on his role. Source: PubMed Central article PMC6220729 on the Soviet health system (secondary)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public ownership works through market prices, so managers follow prices in running hospitals and clinics, while a central board sets the rules and the investment for care. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that managers follow prices, so a hospital that covers its costs may cut care that earns little, and a central board that sets investment may fund some regions and starve others. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Lange and Taylor, On the Economic Theory of Socialism (1938; Lange's essays date from 1936-1937)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that distribution follows each person's need once classes have disappeared, so anyone who is ill is treated free of charge, as a claim of need rather than a payment. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state withers away only after classes disappear, so while the state still controls care the doctrine gives no fixed rule for funding it, and officials rather than need may decide who is treated. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Marx, Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public ownership of key sectors runs alongside markets, so public hospitals keep core care while markets and special zones add services, with prices reformed gradually under party direction. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that prices move gradually under party direction, so core care may stay cheap while other services are left to fees, and patients who cannot pay for services outside the core may be turned away. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Naughton, The Chinese Economy (2007)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that councils of workers and consumers plan through repeated proposals, so health services and their funding are proposed by the people who use and staff them, and jobs are balanced in complexity. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that neither markets nor central planners allocate, so health funding depends on repeated rounds of proposals, which may be slow, and urgent care may wait while councils agree budgets. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Albert and Hahnel, Looking Forward (1991)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that employers and unions are organised into state-controlled corporations, so care is funded through insurance run by those bodies, with each trade covered by its own scheme under state direction. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state directs industry toward national goals, including war, so health spending may be cut or redirected to military production, and care for groups the state does not favour is left thin. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Italian corporative law (1934)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that interest is prohibited and zakat redistributes wealth, so care is funded through shared-profit finance and zakat, with trust underpinning the contracts that pay for it. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that zakat and trust carry the load, so if donors are few or trust breaks down, funds for care may run short, and the poor who depend on zakat may have no insured route to treatment. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chapra, Towards a Just Monetary System (1985)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that economic life serves well-being, so care is provided through small, local and non-violent arrangements, and moderate spending keeps care within what the community can afford. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production is small-scale and local, so pooled health funds may stay too small to spread risk, and a serious illness can ruin a household that has no larger fund to draw on. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Schumacher, Buddhist Economics (first published 1966)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that widespread property and small enterprise spread the means of care, so families and local bodies keep their own mutual funds, and subsidiarity keeps decisions with the smallest competent body. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a just wage and widespread property are the aim, so a health system that depends on small firms may leave workers in firms too small to offer cover, and local bodies may lack funds for a large illness. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Leo XIII, Rerum Novarum (1891)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a social floor covers everyone within planetary limits, so care is guaranteed to all without growth, with health spending held inside a fixed budget set by that floor. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there is no growth imperative, so a fixed health budget may be held flat while costs rise with age and new treatments, and waiting lists may lengthen as the floor is kept low. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Daly, Steady-State Economics (1977)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that every citizen receives an unconditional income, so people pay for their own care from it, and the income is funded by taxes on land and natural resources. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the income is unconditional, so a fixed payment may not cover serious illness, and people who spend it on other needs may have nothing left for care, with no targeted health cover in place. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Paine, Agrarian Justice (1797)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a government which issues its own currency can fund full employment, so the state can pay for health care from its own currency and set health spending by the limit that inflation sets. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that inflation, not debt, is the real limit, so if spending on care outruns the economy's capacity, prices may rise with the cost of care, and the state may have no clear limit to set. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kelton, The Deficit Myth (2020)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a community sharing a resource makes and enforces its own rules, so a local group may pool funds for care and monitor who draws on them, with rules nested in wider institutions. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that communities design and enforce their own rules, so a small pool may exclude outsiders or fall short when members are few, and local rules may not reach people who move away. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons (1990)

compromise.summary: One national scheme covers every resident, paid for from general taxation and earmarked wage contributions, with basic care free at the point of use. Charges for basic care need a parliamentary vote, and a yearly public test of coverage and out-of-pocket spending checks the scheme.
compromise.details: Keeps: tax-funded care free at the point of use, from The National Health Service, 1948 (Fabian socialism, Nordic social democracy); one national purchaser covering nearly all people, from Taiwan's national health insurance from 1995 (Developmental state); social insurance for sickness, from Germany's sickness insurance law of 1883 (Social market economy); and a compulsory savings account for health care, from Singapore's MediSave account from 1984 (Monetarist neoliberalism). Blocks: charges added during budget cuts, safeguarded by a parliamentary vote; purchaser favouritism, safeguarded by published prices and an annual independent audit; loss of cover through cuts, safeguarded by a fixed coverage floor; inpatient-heavy care, safeguarded by a ring-fenced primary care budget. Test: coverage share, out-of-pocket share of spending, waiting times and clinic visits, every year from launch. Source: Warwick University Library (secondary); Deutschlandmuseum calendar entry for 1 December 1883; BMC Health Services Research (2010); Dollars and Sense on MediSave (secondary); PubMed Central PMC6220729 (secondary); Johnson (1982) and Harvey (2005), model sources for inferred safeguards.
